question: At the start of a fever you often shiver and feel freezing, even though your body temperature is actually rising. What has your brain just done?
source_excerpt: when the hypothalamic set point is suddenly raised, by causes such as pyrogenic substances, chills follow

extra.why_interesting: It seems backwards to shiver and feel freezing while your temperature is actually rising. The answer is that the brain has turned up its internal thermostat, so your normal temperature now registers as too cold.
extra.verification_notes: Chills at fever onset occur because the hypothalamic set point is raised, so the body shivers to reach it; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chills

explanation: The brain resets its target temperature higher to fight infection, so your normal temperature suddenly feels too cold and your muscles shiver to heat you up. When the fever breaks the thermostat drops again, which is why you then sweat.

question: When a frightened cat puffs its tail up like a bottle brush, tiny muscles are pulling its hairs upright. The very same reflex happens to you. What do you call it when it happens on your skin?
source_excerpt: tiny muscles at the base of each hair

extra.why_interesting: Players think of a cat's bottle-brush tail as a cat-only defence display and goosebumps as a quirky human skin thing. Realising they are the same reflex, and that goosebumps are our 'puff-up' with too little fur to show it, gives a satisfying 'oh, of course!' moment.
extra.verification_notes: Goosebumps are the skin manifestation of piloerection, caused by arrector pili muscles pulling hairs upright, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goose_bumps.

explanation: In furry animals this reflex makes them look bigger to a threat and traps warm air in the fur. We've lost most of our fur, so all we get is a skin full of little bumps, which is why fear and cold both give you goosebumps.
